title: Controlling the centre

D0.outcome: Explains that central control means influence over the central squares by pawns or pieces, and that pawns on e4 and d4 are one way and not the only way.

D1.outcome: Told to fight for the centre, picks the move that adds most to control of d4/e4/d5/e5 and names the pieces involved.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, decides whether to capture, support or ignore a central pawn offer by checking whether lines open for his pieces.

D3.outcome: Predicts how an exchange that gives up a central pawn can increase influence (opening the d-file and a diagonal), and when it cannot.

misconceptions: Pawns on e4 and d4 are the same as control of the centre.
Always take the offered centre pawn.
conditions: The pieces can actually exert the pressure and the opponent's pawns are put under restraint.
You are not behind in development and can recapture; what counts is opening lines toward the centre for your pieces.
contrasts: Removing the enemy centre pawn while keeping your own does not give control; the mechanical capture lets the opponent seize a commanding central square.
'control of at least two or three centre squares is needed for any violent attack' (contested by flank-attack practice).

soft_prereq_notes.OPN.TEMPO.D1: central control often comes from gaining tempi
